t: Check if All the Integers in a Range Are Covered — Sweep a Difference Array Across the Query Window
o: We are given up to 50 inclusive intervals with endpoints between 1 and 50, plus a query window [left, right]. We must decide whether EVERY integer x with left <= x <= right lies inside at least one interval. In Example 1 (ranges = [[1,2],[3,4],[5,6]], left = 2, right = 5): 2 is covered by [1,2], 3 and 4 by [3,4], and 5 by [5,6], so the answer is true. In Example 2 (ranges = [[1,10],[10,20]], query [21,21]): 21 sits beyond both intervals, so the answer is false. The tiny constraints mean even checking every point against every interval passes easily, but the natural upgrade — stamping intervals onto a timeline and sweeping once — scales far better and is worth presenting.
k: An integer x is covered iff at least one interval contains it, so interval coverage decomposes into point-by-point membership tests.
A difference array records +1 at each interval start and -1 just past each interval end; a running sum during a left-to-right sweep gives the number of intervals covering each integer.
With all values bounded by 50 the brute force is already fast, but the sweep pattern generalizes to thousands of intervals or huge coordinate windows.

a.i: Translate the definition literally: walk through every integer x in [left, right] and search all intervals for one containing x. If any point has no covering interval, return false immediately. With at most 50 points and 50 intervals this is at most 2500 cheap comparisons.
s: For each x from left to right, scan every range [start, end].
If start <= x <= end, the point is covered; move to the next point.
If no interval covers x, return false.
Return true if the loops finish without failure.
a.t: O(U x n) where U = right - left + 1 <= 50 and n <= 50 — every point is checked against every interval.

a.i: Stamp each interval onto a coordinate line: add 1 where it starts and subtract 1 just past its end. Sweeping left to right while keeping a running sum yields, for every integer, how many intervals currently cover it. Any queried point whose running sum is 0 exposes an uncovered integer, ending the search early.
s: Build diff of size 52; for each [start, end] do diff[start]++ and diff[end + 1]--.
Sweep x from 1 to 50, adding diff[x] to a running counter.
If left <= x <= right while the counter is 0, x is uncovered — return false.
a.t: O(n + U) — one pass over the intervals plus one sweep of the 50 possible coordinates.
a.sp: O(1) — the difference array has a fixed size of 52.

w: State the brute force first — the constraints (everything <= 50) invite it — then offer the difference array as the scalable generalization. The classic pitfall is inclusivity: the cancel entry goes at end + 1, not at end, otherwise the endpoint itself appears uncovered. Only whether the counter is zero matters, so overlapping identical intervals cause no issues. Likely follow-ups: report the uncovered points themselves (collect them during the sweep), or handle coordinates up to 10^9 (coordinate compression or sorting and merging intervals).
